title: Oy, the Candles Are Gone!
summary: On the eighth night of Hanukkah, Dad opens the candle box and it's empty! "Oy, oy, oy, the candles are gone!" The family searches the whole house, and Yoav and Ella suggest a flashlight, fireflies, even bringing down the moon with a ladder. Then someone knocks at the door... and it turns out who took all the candles. A funny rhyming story about lighting with olive oil, just like in the Temple.
pages:
On the eighth night of Hanukkah, when the sky had turned black,
Dad opened the candle box, peeked in, looked... and stepped back. "Kids?"
In the box: nothing. Not one single candle. Just a crumb of wax. And quiet.
Oy, oy, oy, the candles are gone!

They searched in the drawer: scissors. They searched in the closet: a sock.
Under the sofa: an old cookie and soap... and a candle? No. And it's evening by the clock.
Oy, oy, oy, the candles are gone!

Yoav ran up with a flashlight: "Here! We'll light this! Click! What a strong, bright light!"
But Dad smiled: "On Hanukkah we need a little flame that dances. Not a flashlight, and not lightning bright."

And Ella shouted: "Fireflies! We'll catch eight in a jar, and one more!"
"In winter?" laughed Mom. "The fireflies are all asleep now, every single one, with a snore."

And Yoav: "The moon! We'll bring it down with a ladder and put it in the window!"
And Ella: "We'll ask the sun to come back! Just for a minute! Why not, you know?"
Oy, oy, oy, the candles are gone!

Then — knock, knock, knock — someone knocked at the door, gently and slow,
and there stood Grandma Malka, the neighbor, with a straw basket... and a bottle... and a knowing look, just so.

"Out of candles?" laughed Grandma Malka. "Then we'll light like in the Temple, with oil, you know!
Olive oil, and nine little cups, and tiny wicks. Well? What do you say? Yes or no?"
"Yes! Yes! Yes!" everyone shouted, and jumped, and danced, and clapped their hands,
and Dad said: "Olive oil? That's the very best there is! The most beautiful way! Twice as grand!"

Yoav poured, Ella put in the wicks, and Dad lit them: eight, and one more, the shamash, standing tall,
and nine little lights danced in the window, like long ago, just like in the Temple, after all.
And everyone sang "Haneirot Halalu," and Grandma Malka sang the loudest, high and sweet,
and outside the window, people stopped, and looked, and smiled at the little lights from the street.

Then baby Uri crawled in, with a toy truck, in a little blue hat,
and the truck was full of candles! Colorful ones! All the candles! Imagine that!
"Uri!" everyone laughed. "So it was you! You had them all along, it's true!"
And Uri clapped his hands and said: "Candle!" and yawned... and fell asleep. Right here. Right on cue.

And the next year, on the first night, when the sky had turned black,
Dad opened a new box, a full one: "We have candles! Lots of them! Kids, look, they're back!"
But then, from behind — vrrrroom! — a little truck drove off... and quiet.
Oy, oy, oy, the candles are gone!
